# 1. Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) Control

The standard parallel continuous-time PID controller algorithm is defined as:

$$u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_{0}^{t} e(\tau) d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

Where:
- $u(t)$ is the controller output signal ($0 - 100\%$).
- $e(t) = SP - PV(t)$ is the instantaneous control error.
- $K_p$, $K_i$, $K_d$ are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains.

::: {.callout-note}
In industrial DCS platforms (e.g., Emerson DeltaV, Honeywell Experion), the ideal gain form is often expressed with Integral Time ($\tau_i$) and Derivative Time ($\tau_d$):
$$u(t) = K_p \left( e(t) + \frac{1}{\tau_i} \int_0^t e(\tau)d\tau + \tau_d \frac{de(t)}{dt} \right)$$
:::

# 2. Discrete Implementation (Velocity Form)

For digital microcontrollers and real-time numerical simulation, the discrete positional PID formulation is converted to velocity form to prevent integral windup and bump-less transfer:

$$\Delta u_k = K_p \left( e_k - e_{k-1} \right) + K_p \frac{\Delta t}{\tau_i} e_k + K_p \frac{\tau_d}{\Delta t} \left( PV_k - 2 PV_{k-1} + PV_{k-2} \right)$$

$$u_k = u_{k-1} + \Delta u_k$$

# 3. Tuning Methodologies

| Method | Response Type | Aggressiveness | Robustness ($M_s$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ziegler-Nichols** | Quarter-decay | High | Low ($M_s > 2.0$) |
| **Cohen-Coon** | Fast disturbance recovery | High | Moderate |
| **AMIGO (Åström-Hägglund)** | Smooth reference tracking | Balanced | High ($M_s \approx 1.4$) |
| **SIMC (Skogestad)** | Modest overshoot | Tunable ($\tau_c$) | Excellent |

# 4. Anti-Windup & Output Limits

When the controller output $u(t)$ hits hard saturation limits ($0\%$ or $100\%$), integral action must freeze (*clamping*) or decay (*back-calculation*):

$$e_{clamped} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } u \ge u_{max} \text{ and } e > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } u \le u_{min} \text{ and } e < 0 \\ e & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
